account_takeover.title: When a friend's account is stolen
account_takeover.body: A message that really comes from your friend's account may not come from your friend. A stolen account is used to ask their contacts for money, because the name and photo make it feel safe. Verify on a different channel before sending anything.
account_takeover.example: "Emergency, send ₹3,000, I'll return it tomorrow" from your friend's number. Call them. If they do not pick up, do not send.

asset_comparison.title: Comparing one thing with another
asset_comparison.body: Nothing is good or bad on its own. Compare on the same four questions: what return, with what risk, how quickly you can get your money out, and what it costs to own. Any one of them alone misleads.
asset_comparison.example: Gold and a fixed deposit can show the same return and still be completely different holdings.

assets_that_earn.title: Assets that earn money
assets_that_earn.body: Some things you buy put money in your pocket: a stall that sells, tools for paid work, a course that raises your pay. Others take money out: running costs, repairs, EMIs. Borrowing for an asset can make sense only if what it earns comfortably covers the repayments.
assets_that_earn.example: A ₹10,000 stall that earns ₹600 a month pays for itself in under a year and a half.

behaviour_gap.title: The behaviour gap
behaviour_gap.body: Most people earn less than the things they invest in, because they buy after a rise and sell after a fall. The gap between what the investment did and what the investor got is made entirely of decisions taken while frightened or excited.
behaviour_gap.example: A fund rose 12% over five years while its average investor got 7% — the difference is buying high and selling low.

bid_ask_liquidity.title: The gap between buying and selling
bid_ask_liquidity.body: At any moment there is a price buyers will pay and a slightly higher price sellers will take. The gap between them is a cost you pay on every trade. In a thinly traded share the gap is wide, and trading often eats the gains.
bid_ask_liquidity.example: Buyers at ₹98, sellers at ₹102: buy and sell immediately and you are 4% down before anything moved.

bnpl.title: Buy now, pay later
bnpl.body: BNPL splits a purchase into instalments. It feels free, but late fees and interest can follow, it counts as borrowing, and it makes it easy to buy wants you can't afford today.
bnpl.example: "Headphones for ₹300 a month!" is still ₹1,200 of headphones, and a debt.

bond_price_rates.title: Bond prices and interest rates
bond_price_rates.body: A bond pays a fixed amount. When new bonds start paying more, the old one is worth less to a buyer, so its price falls — and the other way around. The payment never changed; what changed is what else was on offer.
bond_price_rates.example: You hold a bond paying ₹80 a year. New bonds pay ₹100. Nobody will pay full price for yours, so its price drops until the deal matches.

bonds.title: Bonds: lending to a government or company
bonds.body: When you buy a bond, you lend money to a government or company for a fixed time and they pay you a fixed interest rate. Government bonds are among the safest investments; returns are lower than stocks but steadier.
bonds.example: Paisapur's town bond pays 8% a year for 1 year. The town uses the money to rebuild the bridge.

budgeting.title: Budgeting with jars
budgeting.body: A budget is a plan for your money before you spend it. A simple version is the 50/30/20 rule: about 50% for needs, 30% for wants and 20% for saving. Adjust the numbers to your life, but always plan saving first.
budgeting.example: With ₹1,500: about ₹750 for needs, ₹450 for wants, ₹300 saved.

commodities.title: Commodities
commodities.body: Gold, silver and oil are things, not businesses. They earn nothing on their own: no profit, no dividend, no rent. The only return is someone later paying more than you did.
commodities.example: A gram of gold produces nothing in a year. A share in a shop might pay a dividend.

commodity_exchange.title: How commodities are traded
commodity_exchange.body: Commodities trade on their own exchanges, in standard units and grades, often as contracts rather than the metal itself. Price moves follow world demand and currency as much as anything local.
commodity_exchange.example: The price on the board is for a standard purity and weight, not for the bangle in the shop.

compound_interest.title: Compound interest
compound_interest.body: With compound interest, you earn interest on your interest too. The longer you leave it, the faster it grows. Time matters more than the amount you start with.
compound_interest.example: ₹10,000 at 8% a year becomes about ₹21,600 in 10 years and about ₹46,600 in 20. The second 10 years earn more than the first.

context_dependence.title: The same thing can be either
context_dependence.body: Whether something is a need depends on your life, not on the object. The same item can be a want one month and a need the next, and nobody can tell you which from outside.
context_dependence.example: A phone recharge is a want — until your classes move online, and then it is how you attend school.

credit_card.title: Credit cards and the minimum payment trap
credit_card.body: A credit card is a short loan. Pay the full bill on time and it's free. Pay only the minimum and the rest is charged interest of around 3–4% a month (over 40% a year), so a small balance can last years.
credit_card.example: ₹10,000 on a card, paying only the minimum, can take years to clear and cost thousands in interest.

credit_score.title: Credit score
credit_score.body: A credit score (in India, usually 300 to 900) shows lenders how reliably you repay. Paying on time raises it; missing payments drops it fast. A good score gets you loans at better rates later.
credit_score.example: Every on-time EMI nudges your score up. One missed EMI can undo months of good behaviour.

default_risk.title: Default risk
default_risk.body: The promise of a return is only as good as whoever makes it. Default risk is the chance the borrower simply cannot pay. A higher promised rate usually means a higher chance of not being paid at all, not a free bonus.
default_risk.example: Two lenders offer 9% and 30%. The 30% is not generosity: it is what the borrower had to promise because nobody safer would lend to them.

delayed_gratification.title: Waiting pays (delayed gratification)
delayed_gratification.body: Buying something now with credit feels great today and costs more tomorrow. Saving for it first means you pay only the price, and you often find you wanted it less than you thought.
delayed_gratification.example: A ₹8,000 phone on a card, paying the minimum, can end up costing ₹10,000 or more. Saved for over 10 months, it costs ₹8,000.

depreciation.title: Depreciation: things lose value
depreciation.body: Phones, bikes and gadgets are worth less every year you own them. If you borrow to buy them, you keep paying for something that keeps shrinking.
depreciation.example: A ₹30,000 bike may be worth about ₹25,000 after a year, while a 2-year loan on it still has a year of EMIs left.

diversification.title: Diversification
diversification.body: Don't put all your eggs in one basket. Spreading money across many companies and kinds of assets means one bad investment can't sink you.
diversification.example: If Gully Gadgets crashes, someone with all their money in it loses badly; someone holding 50 companies barely notices.

dividends.title: Dividends
dividends.body: Some companies hand part of their profit to shareholders as a dividend. It is cash in your pocket without selling anything. A company can cut or skip it in a bad year — a dividend is a decision, not a promise.
dividends.example: 100 shares paying ₹4 each gives you ₹400, whether or not the share price moved that year.

education_loan.title: Education loans
education_loan.body: Education loans pay for courses and degrees, often at lower interest than other loans, and repayment usually starts after the course. They can be good debt when the course really improves what you can earn. Always try scholarships first.
education_loan.example: Paisapur Bank's education loan charges 0.8% a month, cheaper than its regular 1% and far cheaper than a moneylender's 5%.

emergency_fund.title: Emergency fund
emergency_fund.body: An emergency fund is money kept only for surprises: a broken phone, a medical bill, a lost job. Aim for 3–6 months of needs, in a place you can reach quickly, like a savings account.
emergency_fund.example: With ₹800 of needs a month, 3 months is ₹2,400. When the phone screen cracks, you pay and stay calm.

emi.title: EMI: equated monthly instalment
emi.body: An EMI is the fixed amount you repay every month, covering both interest and principal. A longer tenure means a smaller EMI but more total interest. Always compare total cost, not just the EMI.
emi.example: ₹30,000 at 1% a month: 12 months = ₹2,665 EMI (₹31,980 total); 24 months = ₹1,412 EMI (₹33,890 total).

etf.title: Exchange-traded funds
etf.body: An ETF is a fund you buy and sell on the exchange like a share. It usually tracks an index and charges less than a managed fund, but every trade carries the exchange's own costs, so frequent trading undoes the saving.
etf.example: The same basket as an index fund, bought through a broker at a live price instead of at the day's closing value.

exchange_basics.title: What an exchange does
exchange_basics.body: An exchange is the marketplace where buyers and sellers of shares find each other. It does not set prices or guarantee anything; it matches orders and records who owns what. The price is just where a buyer and a seller agreed.
exchange_basics.example: Nobody decided the share was worth ₹240. Someone offered ₹240, someone accepted, and that became the price.

expense_tracking.title: Where it actually went
expense_tracking.body: Small amounts do not feel like spending, so they never get counted. Counting them is the only way to see them. The problem is almost never one big purchase.
expense_tracking.example: ₹20 of chai a day is ₹440 a month, and ₹5,280 a year. Nobody remembers spending ₹5,280 on chai.

fake_kyc.title: Fake KYC updates
fake_kyc.body: KYC means the bank already knows who you are. A real bank never asks you to finish it through a link in an SMS, and never asks for your PIN or OTP to do it. A message that says your account closes today unless you tap a link is the scam, not the deadline.
fake_kyc.example: "KYC expired. Account blocked in 24 hours. Update here." Nothing is expiring. Open your bank's own app, or walk into the branch and ask.

fake_support.title: Fake customer care numbers
fake_support.body: Scammers buy ads and seed search results with helpline numbers that look official. Whoever answers will ask you to install a screen-sharing app, read out an OTP, or make a small "test" payment. Real support never needs any of those.
fake_support.example: Your payment failed, so you search for the helpline and call the first number. Use the number printed inside the official app instead.

fees.title: Fees eat returns
fees.body: A small yearly fee looks harmless, but it's taken every year from your whole investment, and compounds against you. Always check the fee (expense ratio).
fees.example: Over 20 years, a 1.5% fee can eat roughly a quarter of what you would have had with a 0.2% fee.

fees_cost.title: Fees are certain, returns are not
fees_cost.body: A fee is taken every year whether the investment did well or badly, and it compounds against you exactly as returns compound for you. A difference of one percent sounds trivial and is not.
fees_cost.example: Over 20 years, 1.5% a year instead of 0.3% takes roughly a fifth of the final amount.

fixed_deposit.title: Fixed deposit (FD)
fixed_deposit.body: In a fixed deposit you lock money in a bank for a set time at a higher interest rate than a savings account. Breaking it early usually costs a penalty. A recurring deposit (RD) does the same with a fixed amount every month.
fixed_deposit.example: Paisapur Bank pays 7% a year on FDs vs 3.5% on savings. Good for money you won't need for a while; not for your emergency fund.

fixed_vs_variable.title: Fixed and changing costs
fixed_vs_variable.body: Some costs are the same every month and arrive whether you plan for them or not — rent, a bus pass, a fee. Others move. Cover the fixed ones first; they are the ones that bite.
fixed_vs_variable.example: Your sister's school fee arrives the same month every year. It is never a surprise, only an un-planned-for one.

fraud_recovery.title: If you get scammed
fraud_recovery.body: Act fast: call India's cybercrime helpline 1930 first (it can freeze money before it moves on), then call your bank to block your account or card, report on cybercrime.gov.in, change your passwords, and tell someone you trust.
fraud_recovery.example: Scammed at 9 pm? Call 1930 and your bank the same night. Don't wait for morning.

goal_setting.title: Money goals
goal_setting.body: A good goal is specific (what), has a number (how much) and a deadline (by when). Split it into a monthly amount so you know if you're on track.
goal_setting.example: "A ₹8,000 phone in 10 months" means saving ₹800 a month. "Save some money" is a wish, not a goal.

gold.title: Gold
gold.body: Gold often holds value when other things fall, and families in India have long saved in it. But it pays no interest, jewellery has making charges, and its price swings too. Many people keep only a small part of their money in gold.
gold.example: Buying a ₹6,000 gold coin as jewellery may cost ₹6,600 with making charges, and sell back for less.

gold_costs.title: What gold actually costs
gold_costs.body: Jewellery carries making charges, the dealer's margin and the gap between buying and selling price, and keeping it safe costs money too. The metal can rise and you can still be behind.
gold_costs.example: Making charges of 10% mean the price has to rise 10% before you break even.

good_bad_debt.title: Good debt and bad debt
good_bad_debt.body: Debt can help when it pays for something that grows your income or value (like education) at a fair rate you can afford. It hurts when it pays for wants, comes at a high rate, or the repayments squeeze your needs.
good_bad_debt.example: An education loan for a course that raises your earning power can be good debt. A loan for a party is bad debt.

gst.title: GST: tax on what you buy
gst.body: Goods and Services Tax is added to most things you buy and goes to the government. Since 2025 most items are taxed at 5% or 18%, and some basics like fresh fruit and notebooks at 0%. The shelf price usually already includes GST.
gst.example: A ₹150 recharge with 18% GST includes about ₹23 of tax. Your bill shows it.

identity_protection.title: Protecting your identity
identity_protection.body: Keep your ID numbers, photos of documents, passwords and OTPs private. Use different passwords, turn on screen locks, and don't install apps from links.
identity_protection.example: A photo of your ID card sent to a stranger can be used to open loans in your name.

impersonation.title: Impersonation calls
impersonation.body: Scammers call pretending to be a bank, the police, a courier or a relative in trouble. They create panic so you act before you think. Hang up and call back on the official number yourself.
impersonation.example: "This is your bank. There's fraud on your account, tell me the OTP to block it." Hang up.

income.title: Income
income.body: Income is money that comes in: an allowance, wages from work, a scholarship, or profit from a business. Some income is fixed (the same every month) and some is irregular (it changes month to month).
income.example: Tutoring pays ₹1,000 in a quiet month and ₹2,400 in exam season. Plan with the low number, not the high one.

income_tax.title: Income tax
income_tax.body: When you start earning, part of your income above a basic limit goes to the government as income tax, in slabs: higher income pays a higher rate on the part above each slab. Taxes pay for roads, schools and hospitals.
income_tax.example: Most students pay no income tax because their income is below the limit, but they still pay GST on purchases.

index_etf.title: Index funds and ETFs
index_etf.body: An index fund simply buys every company in a market index (like the top companies of a stock exchange) instead of picking. An ETF is a fund you buy and sell on the exchange like a share. Both are usually cheap and well diversified.
index_etf.example: The Deccan 5 Index ETF holds all five Deccan companies for a fee of just 0.2% a year.

index_investing.title: Tracking the index
index_investing.body: An index fund does not try to pick winners; it holds the whole list in the same proportions. That sounds unambitious, and over long periods it beats most funds that do try, mainly because it costs so much less.
index_investing.example: No manager, no star picks — just the index, minus a small fee.

inflation.title: Inflation
inflation.body: Inflation is prices rising over time, so the same money buys less. In India prices have often risen around 4–6% a year. Money that earns less than inflation is quietly shrinking.
inflation.example: Chai that cost ₹10 a few years ago costs ₹15–20 now. Watch Zaroorat Store's prices creep up month by month.

informal_lending.title: Moneylenders and informal loans
informal_lending.body: Informal lenders are fast and need no papers, but often charge 3–10% a month (36–120% a year) and may use pressure to collect. Banks and registered lenders are slower but much cheaper and follow rules.
informal_lending.example: 5% a month sounds small. On ₹10,000 that's ₹500 every month, ₹6,000 a year.

insurance.title: Insurance: sharing risk
insurance.body: Insurance pools small payments (premiums) from many people to pay the few who face a big loss. You pay a little for sure to avoid a huge loss maybe. Health and term life insurance protect families from disasters.
insurance.example: ₹100 a month for insurance feels wasted until the month your stall burns down.

interest_compound.title: Compound interest
interest_compound.body: Compound interest is paid on the original amount plus everything it has already earned. Each period starts from a slightly bigger number, so the growth curves upward instead of running straight.
interest_compound.example: ₹10,000 at 8% compounded earns ₹800, then ₹864, then ₹933 — because the second year earns interest on ₹10,800, not ₹10,000.

interest_simple.title: Simple interest
interest_simple.body: Simple interest is paid on the original amount only, every period, and never on the interest already earned. It grows in a straight line.
interest_simple.example: ₹10,000 at 8% simple interest earns ₹800 every year: ₹800, ₹1,600, ₹2,400 after three years. Always ₹800.

irregular_income.title: When income changes
irregular_income.body: Tutoring, shop sales and gig work rise and fall. Even an allowance can shrink when the family has a hard month. Plan with your lowest normal month and let good months fill your savings.
irregular_income.example: If you earn ₹1,000 in a bad month and ₹2,400 in a good one, budget for ₹1,000 and save the rest.

job_scam.title: Fake job and task scams
job_scam.body: Real jobs pay you; they never ask you to pay to join. "Earn ₹5,000 a day liking videos" offers are scams that pay a little at first to win trust, then ask for bigger "deposits".
job_scam.example: "Pay ₹500 registration fee to start the part-time job" is the tell.

kyc.title: KYC: Know Your Customer
kyc.body: Before opening an account, a bank must check who you are with an identity proof and an address proof, plus a photo. Students under 18 can open a minor account with a parent or guardian.
kyc.example: Real banks ask for KYC at the branch or in their official app. They never ask you to "update KYC" through a link in an SMS.

lending_as_investing.title: Lending is investing
lending_as_investing.body: When you lend, you are investing: you hand over money now for a promise of more later. Everything that makes lending risky — who the borrower is, whether they can pay — is exactly what makes an investment risky.
lending_as_investing.example: Lending ₹5,000 to a shop that pays back ₹5,500 in a year is a 10% investment, with the shop's survival as the risk.

lending_to_friends.title: Lending to friends and family
lending_to_friends.body: Only lend what you could afford to never get back. Agree on when it will be repaid. Saying no kindly is allowed.
lending_to_friends.example: Lending ₹500 out of ₹3,000 is fine. Lending your whole emergency fund is not.

liquidity.title: Liquidity
liquidity.body: Liquidity is how quickly you can turn something into money at a fair price. Cash is perfectly liquid, a listed share nearly so, a room full of stock or a plot of land much less. An emergency does not wait for a buyer.
liquidity.example: Shares sell in minutes. A shop's unsold stock might take months, and only at a discount.

loan_app_trap.title: Predatory loan apps
loan_app_trap.body: Illegal loan apps promise instant money with no checks, then cut huge "processing fees", charge very high interest, and harass you and your contacts. Only borrow from lenders registered with the regulator, and never give an app access to your contacts and photos.
loan_app_trap.example: "₹5,000 instantly!" You receive ₹4,000 and owe ₹5,000 plus 4% a month.

loan_basics.title: How a loan works
loan_basics.body: A loan has a principal (the amount borrowed), an interest rate, a tenure (how long) and sometimes fees. The total cost is everything you pay back minus what you received.
loan_basics.example: Borrow ₹10,000 at 1% a month for 12 months: you pay back about ₹10,660. The ₹660 is the cost of borrowing.

market_cap.title: Market capitalisation
market_cap.body: A company's market value is its share price times the number of shares. A high price per share does not mean a big company — a small company can have few, expensive shares, and a huge one can have many cheap ones.
market_cap.example: ₹50 × 10 crore shares is a bigger company than ₹2,000 × 1 lakh shares, by a long way.

minimum_balance_fees.title: Minimum balance
minimum_balance_fees.body: A minimum balance is money you must leave sitting in the account at all times. Dip below it, even once, and the bank takes a fee. It is not a saving — it is money you cannot use.
minimum_balance_fees.example: ₹1,000 locked away out of a ₹800 allowance is not a savings plan. It is a monthly fine waiting to happen.

mutual_funds.title: Mutual funds
mutual_funds.body: A mutual fund pools money from many people and a professional manager invests it in many stocks or bonds. You get instant diversification with a small amount, but you pay a yearly fee.
mutual_funds.example: Star Picks Fund charges 1.5% a year to try to beat the market. Most active funds don't, over the long run.

needs_wants.title: Needs and wants
needs_wants.body: Needs are things you must have to live, study and work: food, transport, basic phone recharge, school supplies. Wants make life nicer but you can live without them. Some things are a need at one price and a want at another.
needs_wants.example: A bus pass is a need. Branded sneakers when your shoes are fine are a want.

net_worth.title: Net worth: assets minus liabilities
net_worth.body: Assets are what you own that has value (cash, savings, investments, a plot of land). Liabilities are what you owe (loans, card balances). Net worth = assets − liabilities. It's the real score of your finances.
net_worth.example: A ₹30,000 bike bought with a ₹30,000 loan adds a ₹30,000 asset that loses value and a ₹30,000 debt that grows with interest.

nominee.title: Nominee
nominee.body: A nominee is the person the bank hands your money to if something happens to you. It takes one line on the form. Without it, your family needs court papers to reach money that was always theirs.
nominee.example: One line at the counter, or months of paperwork later. Same money either way.

opportunity_cost.title: Opportunity cost
opportunity_cost.body: Every rupee can only be spent once. The opportunity cost of a choice is the best thing you gave up to make it.
opportunity_cost.example: The ₹1,800 sneakers cost you more than ₹1,800: they also cost 2 months of progress towards your phone.

paper_vs_realised.title: On paper, or in your hand
paper_vs_realised.body: A price going up does not put money in your pocket. The gain is on paper until you actually sell; until then it can still disappear. The same is true of a fall: it is not a loss you have taken until you sell.
paper_vs_realised.example: Your shares are worth ₹5,000 today against the ₹4,000 you paid. You have not made ₹1,000 — you have ₹1,000 of paper gain that next month may be ₹600.

pay_yourself_first.title: Pay yourself first
pay_yourself_first.body: Don't save whatever is left at the end of the month: there is usually nothing left. Move your saving out the day money arrives, ideally automatically, then live on the rest.
pay_yourself_first.example: A standing instruction to move ₹200 into your goal pot every month means you save without having to remember.

phishing.title: Phishing messages
phishing.body: Phishing messages pretend to be a bank, a company or the government to make you click a link or share details. Their tells: urgency, threats, strange links, spelling mistakes, and asking for secrets.
phishing.example: "Your account will be BLOCKED today. Update KYC at this link" has urgency, a threat and a link. Delete it and call the bank's official number.

pin_secrecy.title: PINs, OTPs and passwords are only yours
pin_secrecy.body: Your PIN, OTP and passwords are the keys to your money. No bank officer, delivery person or friend ever needs them. Anyone who asks is trying to take your money.
pin_secrecy.example: "Sir, tell me the OTP to stop the fraud" is the fraud.

ponzi.title: Ponzi and pyramid schemes
ponzi.body: A Ponzi scheme pays early investors with money from new investors, not real profits. It looks like it works, until new money stops and it collapses. Most people lose everything.
ponzi.example: "Double Dhamaka" pays the first members on time. That's what makes everyone else join.

pooled_funds.title: Pooled funds
pooled_funds.body: A fund collects money from many people and buys a basket of things with it. For a small amount you get a spread you could not afford alone, and someone else does the buying — for a fee.
pooled_funds.example: ₹500 buys a slice of a basket of thirty companies; ₹500 of a single share buys two shares of one.

profit_loss.title: Profit and loss
profit_loss.body: Profit is what you have left after you take away what you paid. Sell something for more than it cost and the difference is profit; sell for less and the difference is a loss. Everything else about investing is a longer version of this one sum.
profit_loss.example: You buy a cricket bat for ₹1,200 and sell it a year later for ₹1,500. Profit ₹300. Sell it for ₹900 instead and you are ₹300 down.

property_costs.title: What property actually costs
property_costs.body: The purchase price is not the cost. Registration, stamp duty, repairs, taxes and the months it may sit empty all come out of the return — and it cannot be sold in a hurry without a discount.
property_costs.example: A flat that rose 40% over ten years may have returned very little after registration, repairs and the agent's cut.

qr_scam.title: QR codes only send money
qr_scam.body: Scanning a QR code and entering your PIN pays money out. Nothing you scan and approve can pull money in. Anyone who sends a QR code so they can "pay you" is trying to take money from you.
qr_scam.example: A buyer sends a QR code to pay for your cycle. Scanning it and entering your PIN sends them the money. Ask them to pay to your UPI ID instead.

real_estate.title: Property (real estate)
real_estate.body: Land and houses can grow in value and earn rent, but they cost a lot, take time to sell (illiquid), and come with taxes, paperwork and upkeep.
real_estate.example: A Paisapur plot costs ₹50,000. If you need money urgently, you can't sell a tenth of a plot.

real_return.title: Real return
real_return.body: Your real return is what you earn after inflation. If savings pay 3.5% and prices rise 6%, your money is actually losing buying power.
real_return.example: Real return ≈ interest rate − inflation. 7% FD − 6% inflation ≈ 1% real growth.

red_flags.title: Reading the red flags
red_flags.body: Almost every scam message carries the same few tells: a deadline, a threat, a reward you did not earn, a link that is nearly the right address, a request for a secret, and a stranger who wants the conversation moved somewhere private. Spotting two of them together is usually enough.
red_flags.example: "Congratulations, you won. Claim in 2 hours. Share OTP to confirm." A prize you never entered, a clock, and a request for a secret: three flags in one line.

return_percent.title: Return as a percentage
return_percent.body: ₹300 of profit means nothing on its own — it depends how much you put in. A percentage return divides the profit by what you paid, so you can compare two very different amounts fairly.
return_percent.example: ₹300 on ₹1,200 is 25%. ₹300 on ₹30,000 is 1%. The same rupees, two very different results.

risk_return.title: Risk and return
risk_return.body: Investments that can earn more usually can also lose more. Safe options (savings, FDs, government bonds) earn less; riskier ones (stocks) can earn more over long periods but swing a lot along the way.
risk_return.example: FD: 7%, steady. Stocks: maybe +25% one year and −15% the next.

rule_of_72.title: The rule of 72
rule_of_72.body: Divide 72 by a yearly interest rate to estimate how many years money takes to double. It works for growth (savings) and for debt (what you owe).
rule_of_72.example: At 8%, money doubles in about 72 ÷ 8 = 9 years. A card charging 36% a year doubles your debt in about 2 years.

sales_tricks.title: Sale tricks
sales_tricks.body: Shops use tricks to make you buy: "today only", "50% off" a price that was inflated first, "buy 2 get 1", and easy EMIs. A sale only saves money if you were going to buy the thing anyway.
sales_tricks.example: "₹3,600 → ₹1,800!" If you didn't need sneakers, you didn't save ₹1,800. You spent ₹1,800.

savings_account.title: Savings account
savings_account.body: A savings account is for keeping money safely and taking it out when you need it. It pays a small interest rate. A current account is for businesses that make many payments and usually pays no interest.
savings_account.example: Your Paisapur Bank savings account pays 3.5% a year: ₹10,000 kept all year earns about ₹350.

scholarships.title: Scholarships
scholarships.body: A scholarship is money for studies that you don't pay back. Government schemes, colleges, NGOs and companies offer them for merit, need or both. Apply early and to many; it's the cheapest money there is.
scholarships.example: A ₹1,500 merit scholarship covers almost a third of a ₹5,000 course, with nothing to repay.

simple_interest.title: Interest
simple_interest.body: Interest is the price of money. When you save, the bank pays you interest. When you borrow, you pay interest. Simple interest = principal × rate × time.
simple_interest.example: ₹1,000 at 6% a year for 2 years earns ₹1,000 × 0.06 × 2 = ₹120 of simple interest.

simple_vs_compound.title: Simple against compound
simple_vs_compound.body: Over one year the two are almost identical, which is why the difference is easy to miss. Over ten or twenty the gap becomes most of the result. Compounding is not a trick; it is what happens when you leave earnings where they are.
simple_vs_compound.example: ₹10,000 at 8% for 20 years: ₹26,000 simple, about ₹46,600 compounded. The extra ₹20,000 is interest earning interest.

sip.title: SIP: investing a fixed amount every month
sip.body: A Systematic Investment Plan invests the same amount every month, whatever the market does. You buy more units when prices are low and fewer when high, and you build the habit.
sip.example: ₹500 a month into an index fund for 10 years. Some months are up, some down; the habit does the work.

sip_concept.title: Investing a little each month
sip_concept.body: Putting in a fixed amount regularly means you buy more units when prices are low and fewer when they are high, without having to guess. It smooths the price you pay. It does not promise a profit.
sip_concept.example: ₹1,000 a month buys 10 units at ₹100 and 12.5 at ₹80 — the average cost ends up below the average price.

speculation_vs_investing.title: Investing or speculating
speculation_vs_investing.body: Investing puts money behind something that earns: a business, a loan, rent. Speculating bets on a price moving, with nothing underneath producing anything. Both can make money; only one has something working for you.
speculation_vs_investing.example: A share in a tiffin business earns from meals sold. A coin that earns nothing only pays if someone later pays more.

start_early.title: Starting early
start_early.body: Years matter more than amounts. Money put in early gets more compounding periods than money put in later, so a small amount started now can beat a larger amount started in ten years.
start_early.example: ₹500 a month from 18 beats ₹1,000 a month from 33, if both stop at 50 — the first had fifteen extra years to compound.

stock_basics.title: What a share is
stock_basics.body: A share is a small piece of ownership in a company. Owning one means a share of whatever the company earns and is worth — and a share of the fall if it does badly. You are a part-owner, not a lender.
stock_basics.example: A company split into 1,000 shares, and you hold 10: you own 1% of it, with no promise attached.

stocks.title: Stocks: owning a piece of a company
stocks.body: A share (stock) is a small piece of ownership in a company. If the company does well, the price can rise and it may share profits as dividends. If it does badly, the price can fall a lot.
stocks.example: Buying 1 share of Pearl City Power makes you a tiny owner of the power company.

time_horizon.title: Time horizon
time_horizon.body: When will you need the money? Money for the next few months belongs somewhere safe (savings, FD). Money for 5+ years can ride out the ups and downs of stocks.
time_horizon.example: Next month's bus pass: savings account. Money for when you are 30: an index fund can make sense.

tips_rumours.title: Tips and rumours
tips_rumours.body: "Buy this stock now, it will double!" tips on social media or chat groups are often wrong, and sometimes a scam where the tipster sells to you. Decide with facts, not hype.
tips_rumours.example: A Telegram channel pushes Gully Gadgets. The people who bought early sell to everyone who joins late.

too_good_to_be_true.title: Too good to be true
too_good_to_be_true.body: Guaranteed high returns, no risk, and pressure to decide fast: that combination is a scam. Real investments never guarantee to double your money quickly.
too_good_to_be_true.example: "Guaranteed 10% a week!" That's over 14,000% a year. No honest investment does that.

uncertainty_ranges.title: Ranges, not single numbers
uncertainty_ranges.body: Nobody can say what an investment will be worth in ten years. An honest projection gives a range and says what it assumed. A single confident number is a sales pitch, not a forecast.
uncertainty_ranges.example: "Between ₹1.4 and ₹2.6 lakh, assuming 8% average growth" is a real answer. "₹2.6 lakh" is not.

upi_basics.title: UPI payments
upi_basics.body: UPI moves money instantly between bank accounts using a phone. To pay, you scan a QR code or enter a UPI ID, check the name, then enter your secret UPI PIN.
upi_basics.example: Always check the name that appears before you enter the PIN. A wrong name means stop.

upi_collect.title: A PIN is for paying, never for receiving
upi_collect.body: You never need to enter your UPI PIN, scan a QR code or approve a request to receive money. If entering your PIN is needed, money is leaving your account.
upi_collect.example: A "buyer" sends a QR code and says "scan it to receive ₹1,500". Scanning and entering the PIN would send them ₹1,500.

volatility.title: Ups and downs (volatility)
volatility.body: Markets go up and down, sometimes sharply. Selling in a panic after a fall locks in the loss. People who stay invested for years have historically been rewarded, but nothing is guaranteed.
volatility.example: The Deccan market falls 15% in a month. The patient investor holds; the panicked one sells at the bottom.

volatility_vs_loss.title: A swing is not a loss
volatility_vs_loss.body: Volatility is how much a price moves about. It feels like danger, but a price that fell and recovered cost you nothing unless you sold at the bottom. The permanent loss is the one you lock in.
volatility_vs_loss.example: A fund that dropped 20% and came back within a year lost money only for those who sold in the dip.

why_bank.title: Why keep money in a bank
why_bank.body: Cash at home can be lost, stolen or spent on a whim. A bank keeps it safe, pays you interest, and lets you pay digitally. In India, deposits are insured up to ₹5 lakh per person per bank if a bank fails.
why_bank.example: ₹1,000 under the mattress is still ₹1,000 next year, if nobody takes it. In a savings account it earns a little extra and is protected.

windfall.title: Windfalls and lump sums
windfall.body: A windfall is unexpected or one-off money: a festival bonus, a gift, a scholarship paid all at once. Because it isn't part of your regular budget, it's easy to spend it all. A good rule: save most of it, enjoy a little.
windfall.example: A ₹3,000 scholarship arrives once a term. Treat it as three to six months of money, not one good weekend.

wrong_transfer.title: The "sent by mistake" trick
wrong_transfer.body: A stranger says money landed in your account by accident and begs you to send it back fast. Often nothing arrived, or it arrived from a stolen account and will be reversed, leaving you short by whatever you sent. Check your own balance first, and let the bank move the money back.
wrong_transfer.example: Your balance has not changed, but the message insists ₹2,000 came in. Do not send anything. Tell the bank and let them sort it out.
